CausalChain: DDR gene alterations → Accumulation of DNA damage → Activation of the cGAS-STING pathway → Production of type I interferons → Upregulation of PD-L1 and recruitment of T cells → Modulation of tumor microenvironment from 'cold' to 'hot' → Increased sensitivity to ICIs; additionally, PARP inhibition reinforces DNA damage and immune signaling.
Hypothesis: In biliary tract cancer, DDR deficiencies activate the cGAS-STING pathway leading to an immunogenic tumor microenvironment characterized by increased PD-L1 expression and T cell infiltration; therefore, combining PARP inhibitors with immune checkpoint inhibitors may synergistically convert immunologically 'cold' BTCs into 'hot' tumors, enhancing the clinical efficacy of immunotherapy.
Abstract: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) are characterized by a hostile tumor microenvironment and variable responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). While individual predictive biomarkers such as PD‐L1, tumor mutational burden (TMB), and MSI/dMMR have been studied, their predictive power in BTC remains inconsistent. Recent insights into DNA damage repair (DDR) gene alterations suggest that even in the presence of low frequency MSI or TMB, disruptions in DDR may trigger innate immune responses via the cGAS-STING pathway, leading to upregulation of PD-L1 and recruitment of cytotoxic T cells. This review hypothesizes that DDR deficiencies in BTC may create an immunologically more active microenvironment, which could be exploited by combining DDR-targeting agents (such as PARP inhibitors) with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors. Such a combination strategy might convert “cold” tumors into “hot” ones and improve therapeutic response. This novel hypothesis should be further investigated in preclinical models and early-phase clinical trials to validate the role of DDR-mediated immune modulation in BTC.
